extracted.intended_audience: scholarly researchers in journalism, political communication, and computational content analysis
extracted.subtask_description: Operationalizing and testing which characteristics of journalistic news articles predict the number of times those articles are shared on social media (Twitter and Facebook) using automated content analysis and regression models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic topic
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an article deals with the own country (domestic issues) versus nondomestic issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesized (H1a) and found to increase shares: articles covering domestic issues are shared more often (e.g., 1.29× on Twitter and 1.80× on Facebook compared with nondomestic issues). Used as a predictor of shareworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographical distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorized distance of the event/topic's location from the Netherlands (several distance bands: e.g., outside the Netherlands but <500 km, <1,000 km, <2,000 km, <5,000 km, <10,000 km).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Closer geographic proximity increases shareability; effect sizes decrease with distance. Included as a predictor/control variable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural distance (Non-Western vs Western)
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator whether a story involves a non-Western country (cultural distance) versus Western countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories about non-Western countries receive fewer shares (example effects: 0.83× on Twitter and 0.69× on Facebook compared with Western baseline), implying cultural similarity increases shareability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of disagreement between individuals or groups and mention of several opposing positions (operationalized following Semetko & Valkenburg, 2000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated by a supervised machine learning (SML) classifier (coding accuracy = 80%, AUC = 0.78). Conflict presence modestly increases shares (IRR ≈ 1.11 Twitter, 1.09 Facebook). Examples of indicators: mention of opposing positions, explicit disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Presence of humanizing aspects: providing human examples and faces, vignettes generating strong feelings, and mentioning how an issue affects individuals or groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operationalized via an SML classifier (coding accuracy = 79%, AUC = 0.78). Human interest strongly increases shares on Facebook (articles shared ~1.33×) but is basically irrelevant for Twitter in this study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Positivity (sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Positivity of an article measured with the SentiStrength algorithm on a 1 (not positive) to 5 (very positive) scale (H4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scale reversed for negativity so both range 1–5. Positivity increases number of shares (overall: 1-point increase → IRR 1.043; Facebook effect stronger: 1.171). SentiStrength reported accuracy: 96.9% when a 1-point difference on the 5-point scale is acceptable. Positivity and negativity are treated as largely independent (r = .16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negativity (sentiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Negativity of an article measured with the SentiStrength algorithm on a 1 (not negative) to 5 (very negative) scale (H5); negativity scale reversed so both scales run 1–5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negativity has a smaller positive effect on shares than positivity (example effects: 1.026× on Twitter and 1.080× on Facebook per 1-point increase). Note independence from positivity and measurement caveats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press agency / Exclusiveness (byline indicator)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an article was written by a news agency (determined by parsing the byline for wire-service initials) versus written by site journalists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpreted as an exclusiveness indicator: agency-written articles receive fewer shares (they receive about two-thirds of Twitter shares of other articles and only 0.28× the Facebook interactions), so nonagency (exclusive/site-authored) articles are more shareworthy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic popularity score (noun-distribution method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Popularity of an article's topic at publication time computed by comparing the distribution of nouns in the article title with distributions of nouns in titles across two-week periods: create popularity weight vectors per period; article score S = mean popularity weights of unique nouns in the article derived from the period's vector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: split study period into 2-week windows, extract nouns with Frog Dutch morphosyntactic analyzer, standardize counts to form popularity weights per noun, compute S as mean weight across article nouns. Effect: on Twitter, highly present topics received fewer shares; on Facebook, the opposite pattern was observed—topic popularity effects differ across platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main topic category (machine-classified)
rubrics_metrics.description: Article's main topic as classified by an SML classifier distinguishing 19 Comparative Agendas Project topics, aggregated to 10 topic categories (defense & foreign affairs; political system; economic policy; social affairs & education; law & order; infrastructure; science & technology; culture & entertainment; weather & disasters; sports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a control variable because different topics systematically receive different numbers of shares. Classifier performance reported as F1 = .71; aggregation to 10 categories reduces variable dimensionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article length
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of the article measured in characters (entered into models centered around its mean).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a control because shorter and longer news stories may be shared differently (Berger & Milkman, 2012).

rubrics_metrics.name: Time (days since t0)
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of days since the beginning of the data collection period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control variable to account for changes in the overall popularity of network sites over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: News-site fixed effects (site dummy variables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dummy variables for each news site to account for different intercepts between sites (parool.nl used as reference category).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Controls for baseline differences in share counts across different news websites (some sites are more popular than others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical modeling choice: negative binomial regression
rubrics_metrics.description: Modeling the count of shares using negative binomial regression due to overdispersed count distribution of shares (few articles receive many shares, many receive few).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation reported via incidence rate ratios (IRRs): IRR > 1 indicates positive effect; IRR < 1 indicates negative effect. Authors compared Poisson and negative binomial models and report superior fit for negative binomial (much higher log likelihood).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifier evaluation metrics (AUC, F1, accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance measures used to evaluate automated coders: AUC for binary classifiers (e.g., conflict/human interest AUC ≈ 0.78), F1 for multiclass topic classifier (F1 = .71), and SentiStrength accuracy (96.9% within 1-point tolerance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these metrics to judge reliability of automated operationalizations; note potential measurement error particularly for abstract concepts like negativity compared with straightforward indicators like news agency byline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational indicators for conflict and human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete textual/coding cues used to define conflict and human interest: conflict indicated by disagreement between individuals/groups and mention of opposing positions; human interest indicated by human examples and faces, emotionally strong vignettes, and mention of effects on individuals/groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These operational indicators were used to train the SML classifiers; see Semetko & Valkenburg (2000) and Burscher et al. (2014) for detailed operationalization and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of effect sizes and platform differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Noting and evaluating how substantial effects are and how they differ by platform (Twitter vs Facebook).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors stress that some predictors (e.g., domestic topic or news-agency indicator) exert larger effects than tone measures (positivity/negativity) and that many effects are more pronounced on Facebook than on Twitter; use caution interpreting effect magnitudes and consider platform affordances.
